hook: He conquered an empire from Greece to India before he was 33, and never lost a battle.

pages.t: A horse no one could ride
pages.x: Alexander was born in Pella in 356 BC, the son of King Philip II of Macedon. As a boy he tamed Bucephalus, a wild horse no one could ride, by turning it to face the sun so it could not see its own shadow. His father told him: "Macedon is too small for you."

At Gordium, in what is now Turkey, stood an ancient ox cart tied with a knot so tangled no one could undo it. Whoever did, people said, would rule Asia. In 333 BC Alexander tried, then drew his sword and sliced it apart. "Cutting the Gordian knot" still means solving a hard problem with one bold stroke.

King at 20, he crossed into Asia in 334 BC with about 40,000 men to attack the vast Persian Empire. He won at the Granicus river, then at Issus, where King Darius III fled and left his family behind, and finally at Gaugamela in 331 BC. Babylon and Persepolis fell, and the empire of Cyrus was his.

In Egypt he was welcomed as pharaoh, and the oracle at Siwa hailed him as son of the god Amun. On the coast he founded a city, Alexandria, which became the greatest city of the ancient world, with its lighthouse and library. He named many more cities after himself, and one after his horse.

pages.t: To the edge of the world
pages.x: He marched on through Persia and Central Asia to India, where in 326 BC he beat King Porus and his war elephants at the Hydaspes river. His soldiers, eight years and thousands of kilometres from home, refused to go farther. Alexander sulked in his tent for three days, then turned back.

In June 323 BC, in Babylon, he fell ill with a fever after a feast and died at 32. Asked who should inherit his empire, he is said to have whispered: "The strongest." His generals fought over it for forty years and split it into kingdoms. His body was taken to Egypt and buried in Alexandria.

In 13 years Alexander built an empire from Greece to India. Greek language, cities and art spread across the Middle East in what we call the Hellenistic age, and generals from Caesar to Napoleon studied his battles.
